\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Visible cameras on surface vessels degrade in fog, low light, glare and noise, and so do their detectors. Re-estimating a detector's batch-normalization statistics at test time needs no labels, but doing so on every frame costs about 0.02 average precision (AP) on clean night frames. The difficulty is deciding which frames to adapt: a dark visible frame may show a dark scene or a failing camera, and a health score of the visible image flags every clean night frame as abnormal. We therefore adapt only when the visible frame looks abnormal and an independent day--night signal reports daylight. In IR-gated batch-normalization adaptation (IG-BN), that signal comes from a co-mounted thermal camera; adaptation uses eight-frame blocks, no gradients and no weight changes, and can run causally. On the Pohang Canal dataset with simulated corruptions, every test was pre-registered. On the development set, IG-BN improved 5 of 60 conditions and worsened none. On a held-out daylight run (thirteen logged scorings), it raised ship AP under fog (+0.037), low light (+0.019), glare (+0.031, with a glare term) and sensor noise (+0.182). An ablation showed whole-network adaptation needs the day--night signal: without it, adaptation lost up to 0.023 AP at night. That signal need not come from the thermal camera: a solar-elevation clock from time and position was never worse than the thermal signal on the development set and was better wherever the thermal image was degraded. On held-out daylight frames, adapting every frame did best; the case for gating rests on night frames.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
Batch normalization, infrared imaging, maritime object detection, sensor fusion, test-time adaptation, thermal imaging, unmanned surface vehicles, visible--infrared detection
\end{IEEEkeywords}

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:1}
Maritime perception for autonomous and crewed surface vessels increasingly pairs a visible camera with a long-wave infrared (thermal) camera, on the assumption that the two fail in different conditions. A missed vessel or buoy is a collision risk, and the conditions that hide one---fog, darkness, glare and sensor noise---are the conditions in which a collision-avoidance system most needs its cameras. Visible imagery degrades in fog, haze, glare, rain, darkness and sensor noise \cite{prasad2017video}. Thermal imagery sees through darkness and glare but fails at thermal crossover, when vessel and water reach the same temperature. Neither failure announces itself. A visible detector trained on clean frames meets a fogged or underexposed frame with activation statistics its BatchNorm layers were not fitted to, and simply returns fewer and worse boxes.

Test-time adaptation of normalization statistics is the cheapest repair available. Replacing or mixing the BatchNorm statistics with those of a test batch \cite{li2017revisiting,schneider2020improving} needs no labels, no gradient computation and no weight changes, and it recovers much of the loss under common corruptions. The hard question is not how to adapt but which frames to adapt. Adapting a frame that was never degraded moves a well-fitted detector away from its training statistics: in a pre-registered ablation on our development set, BN-mix applied to every frame gained on corrupted day frames but cost 0.0101 ship AP on clean day frames and 0.0195 on clean night frames (Section~\ref{sec:5.1}). On our held-out daylight run, adapting every frame did not hurt clean frames, so the demonstrated harm of ungated adaptation is at night. Existing selective methods decide which samples to adapt from the model's own outputs or features (Section~\ref{sec:2}). A single visible camera faces an ambiguity that such signals do not resolve: a dark frame may show a dark scene, which the detector was trained on, or a degraded camera, which it was not. Our visible health score, fitted on clean day frames, flags all 1,032 clean night frames of our development set as unhealthy and none of the 1,200 clean day frames (Section~\ref{sec:4.1}).

A thermal camera can answer the question with a different sensor. Our method, IR-gated BatchNorm adaptation (\mbox{IG-BN}), adapts the visible detector only when three conditions hold: the visible frame looks unhealthy, the thermal frame reads daylight, and the thermal frame is itself healthy (Fig.~\ref{fig:1}). A dark visible frame that the thermal camera places in daylight is treated as a degraded camera and adapted; one it places at night is left alone. The thermal reading is a statistic of the thermal image after the dataset's per-frame 8-bit stretch, not a radiometric measurement, and a pre-registered ablation finds that a solar-elevation clock supplies the same day--night information at least as well on this data (Section~\ref{sec:5.1}, Section~\ref{sec:7}).

Our contributions are:

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{IR-gated test-time adaptation for visible--infrared detection.} A label- and gradient-free adaptation of the visible detector, gated per frame by the thermal camera's reading of illumination and by both streams' frame health (Section~\ref{sec:4}). It has a causal form for live streams (\mbox{IG-BN-causal}), a glare term (\mbox{IG-BN+glare}), and an ensemble form (\mbox{IG-BN+ens}); Table~\ref{tab:22} defines every variant. We found no prior test-time adaptation for visible--infrared detection in which the thermal camera decides, without gradients, when to adapt the visible detector (Section~\ref{sec:2}).
\item \textbf{Pre-registered evidence on development and one held-out run.} Every variant was registered before any of its numbers existed. Six variants passed development on 60 cells with no cell worse; a seventh (\mbox{IG-BN-stale}) failed and was dropped. On a held-out daylight run, none of the six was worse than its baseline on any cell. Under fog (+0.0370 ship AP), low light (+0.0186) and glare with the glare term (+0.0309), the held-out gains have the same direction as on development. Sensor noise (+0.1823 [+0.1733, +0.1916]), rain and blur were not in the development grid, so those results are first tests (Section~\ref{sec:5}).
\item \textbf{Negative results from the same system.} We reached this design by elimination. Predicted box uncertainty is informative about which boxes are right but does not improve the fusion; an image-statistic veto that dropped the visible stream at night cost 0.1847 ship AP once the detector was retrained on corrected labels; and no learned gate beat switching that veto off (Section~\ref{sec:6}).
\end{enumerate}

Adverse conditions are simulated, from a camera-chain model for fog, low light and glare and from ImageNet-C-style severities for noise, rain and blur. The data are from a canal and port route, not open sea. The held-out run is all daylight, and each of its cells corrupts one stream at a time, so it tests the gate's visible term, not its day--night decision (Section~\ref{sec:7}).

\section{Related work}\label{sec:2}
\textbf{How test-time adaptation repairs a detector.} AdaBN \cite{li2017revisiting} replaces BatchNorm statistics with those of the test batch, and BN-mix \cite{schneider2020improving}, which we use unchanged, mixes them with the source statistics at a prior strength N. DUA \cite{mirza2022the} updates the statistics online with a decaying momentum and is evaluated on detection. TENT \cite{wang2021tent} and ActMAD \cite{mirza2023actmad} instead update parameters by gradient, minimizing entropy or aligning activation statistics at many layers; ActMAD applies to detectors. Because adapting where nothing shifted can hurt, some methods select which samples to adapt: SuMi \cite{guo2025smoothing} adapts only samples that pass feature-quartile and entropy tests. Others limit adaptation to some layers or weight source against test statistics per layer \cite{yang2022testtime,lim2023ttn,su2024unraveling,liao2024improving}; our gate-free variant (Section~\ref{sec:5.1}) combines both ideas.

\textbf{How multimodal methods decide what to adapt.} Several methods adapt only the shifted modality or reweight toward the reliable one. All of them decide from the model's own predictions or features and update parameters by gradient; they differ in the selection signal. TSA \cite{chen2025testtime} learns a router that chooses which modality to adapt, and reports negative transfer when an unshifted modality is adapted, the failure our gate guards against. AdaPGC \cite{xu2026multimodal} uses the divergence of each modality's prediction from the fused prediction, DASP \cite{he2026decoupling} the redundancy of the fused features, and CARAT \cite{mohapatra2026sourcelearned} each stream's own clean statistics; CARAT argues that cross-modal agreement misleads when sensors measure different physical processes. READ \cite{yang2024testtime}, ABPEM \cite{zhao2025attention} and MM-TTA \cite{shin2022mmtta} reweight the modalities inside the model, through attention or cross-modal pseudo-labels. These methods are evaluated on audio--video classification, sentiment, image--text classification, wearable time series and segmentation. The closest in sensors, Night-TTA \cite{liu2024testtime}, adapts night color--thermal segmentation by training BatchNorm affine parameters against an ensemble teacher, on every night frame, without deciding which frames to adapt.

\textbf{How visible--infrared detectors use illumination and uncertainty.} Illumination-aware fusion is established in multispectral pedestrian detection. IAF R-CNN \cite{li2019illuminationaware} weights its color and thermal sub-networks by an illumination estimate from the color image, and MBNet \cite{zhou2020improving} reweights and aligns modality features by illumination. ProbEn \cite{chen2022multimodal} fuses color and thermal detections by probabilistic ensembling. UA-CMDet \cite{sun2022dronebased} weights each object's training loss by cross-modal box overlap and RGB illumination, and at inference scales the RGB branch's scores by an illumination weight before non-maximum suppression. \citet{zhao2024uncertaintyaware} weight the visible and infrared branch losses by a label uncertainty estimated during training. All of these use illumination or uncertainty to set fusion weights, not to adapt a detector. Gaussian YOLOv3 \cite{choi2019gaussian} attaches per-coordinate variance to a single-stage detector; we use its head (Section~\ref{sec:6.1}).

\textbf{Maritime detection.} Maritime YOLO variants such as RDSC-YOLOv4 \cite{liu2021sea} and YOLOv7-Sea \cite{zhao2023yolov7sea} report accuracy without uncertainty or adaptation. Benchmarks for unmanned surface vehicles, MaSTr1325 \cite{bovcon2019the}, MODS \cite{bovcon2022mods} and LaRS \cite{zust2023lars}, are visible-only. The Pohang Canal dataset \cite{chung2023pohang} with PoLaRIS annotations \cite{choi2025polaris} provides paired visible--thermal maritime video with boxes on both streams; the Singapore Maritime Dataset \cite{prasad2017video} pairs visible with near-infrared video that need not show the same scene, and MassMIND \cite{nirgudkar2023massmind} is thermal only.

\textbf{The gap this paper addresses.} We found no test-time adaptation method for visible--infrared object detection among these papers. Ours differs from the multimodal methods in three ways: the thermal camera decides \emph{whether} to adapt the visible detector, from a statistic of its own image rather than from agreement between model outputs; no gradient is computed and no weight changes; and every variant was registered before it was scored. Selective adaptation of the corrupted modality is not our contribution, and neither is illumination-aware gating by itself, which IAF R-CNN and UA-CMDet apply to fusion weights.

\section{Setting}\label{sec:3}
\subsection{Data}\label{sec:3.1}
The Pohang Canal dataset \cite{chung2023pohang} records a 7.5 km route through a canal, a port and near-coastal water, not open sea, with a visible camera at 2048$\times$1080 and a thermal camera at 640$\times$512, both at 10 Hz. PoLaRIS \cite{choi2025polaris} supplies ship and buoy boxes on both streams. There are five runs: pohang00 (day), pohang01 (night), and pohang02 to pohang04 (day). On disk they hold 158,319 images, 1,183,736 boxes and 28,388 paired visible--infrared frames. The two cameras are not co-registered: frames are paired by nearest timestamp, and the measured residual misalignment is a median of 3--6 px per run. Visible frames are letterboxed to 640$\times$640; thermal frames are delivered as 8-bit images by per-frame min--max normalization, and the 14-bit radiometric values are not recoverable. Splits are interleaved contiguous blocks with guard bands, identical across modalities, and the night labels are the corrected set from a pre-registered restoration of boxes deleted from dark frames (Section~\ref{sec:6.2}).

\subsection{Detectors and fusion}\label{sec:3.2}
Both streams use YOLO26-m \cite{jocher2026ultralytics}: the visible detector with two classes, the thermal detector with a single ship class and a P2 neck, because it cannot see buoys. The backbone was chosen on a 93-run benchmark (Section~\ref{sec:3.5}). We use five independently trained system pairs (visible seed k with thermal seed k), trained on the corrected labels with the held-out run removed from every list, and report the mean over the five.

The baseline fusion is \textsc{union}. Both streams pass to Weighted Boxes Fusion \cite{solovyev2021weighted} at IoU 0.85 with constant stream weights (the visible weight, 0.9926, is the constant the designed uncertainty weighting produced on every frame, Section~\ref{sec:6.1}), and a box whose other-stream partner overlaps it at IoU 0.30 has its score multiplied by 1.5. At this threshold only 0.05 percent of visible boxes find a thermal partner, so the fusion is concatenation with a support bonus. The shipped system, \textsc{shipped}, is \textsc{union} plus a veto that drops the visible stream when the thermal camera indicates night and the visible frame reads dark or veiled. A registered study of replacements for that veto found that switching it off improves on it and that no gate we registered beats \textsc{union} (Section~\ref{sec:6.3}); \textsc{union} is therefore the baseline every adaptation is measured against. \textsc{full\_tta} is the strongest system that changes no detector: five checkpoints per stream, each run on the raw and the horizontally flipped frame, merged per stream by WBF at IoU 0.55, with non-local-means denoising of thermal frames that fail their health check, and no veto. It costs ten detector passes per stream per frame.

\subsection{Corruptions}\label{sec:3.3}
Adverse conditions are simulated on the content rows of each frame. Fog, low light and glare follow a camera-chain model in physical order: atmosphere, optics, sensor noise, exposure, the dataset's own infrared stretch and quantization. Fog is Koschmieder attenuation in linear radiance on per-frame metric depth \cite{sakaridis2018semantic} from Depth Anything V2 \cite{yang2024depth}. Low light is exposure scaling to the real night level, with the night noise measured on training frames. Glare is a source placed against the frame's computed horizon, with spread and exposure response fitted to the one real sun-entry event in training. Sensor noise, rain and motion blur are ImageNet-C-style severities \cite{hendrycks2019benchmarking} with no physical anchor. An earlier off-the-shelf corruption set was found broken at the source (its fog was a fixed 21-px blur) and retired. Sun glint, spray and salt on the lens were not modeled.

\subsection{Evaluation and statistics}\label{sec:3.4}
\textbf{Terms.} A \emph{cell} is one combination of visible condition, thermal condition and, on development, day or night. A \emph{draw} is one random realization of a corruption. VIS and IR denote the visible and infrared (thermal) streams scored alone. \emph{The no-loss property} is fused $\geq$ max(VIS, IR): the fused output scores at least as well as the better single stream.

\textbf{Development.} 2,232 paired validation frames, 1,200 by day (pohang00, 02, 03) and 1,032 by night (pohang01). The grid crosses five visible conditions (clean, fog at severities 1 and 2, low light, glare) with six thermal conditions (clean, fog at severities 1--3, noise at severities 2--3), by day and by night: 60 cells. It contains no visible noise, rain or blur. Corrupted cells average three draws per system; a cell's value is the mean over the five systems, with a 95 percent t-interval (df 4) on paired deltas.

\textbf{Held-out.} pohang04, an all-daylight run of 12,482 frame pairs, was never scored by any fusion system before a single pre-registered look, and neither the five system pairs nor their reference statistics were fitted on it. It has no thermal labels, so every held-out number is scored against the visible ground truth (156,652 boxes). Nine cells corrupt one stream at a time with four fresh draws each (visible fog, low light, sensor noise, rain and blur with clean thermal; clean visible with thermal fog, noise and blur; and clean/clean), and a tenth, visible glare, was added for the glare term. Held-out intervals are paired moving-block bootstraps over frames (block 20 frames, 1,000 replicates) around the five-system mean, because frames at 10 Hz are autocorrelated and a frame-level bootstrap halves the true width. They carry frame-sampling variance only, not variance over systems or draws, so they are not directly comparable with the development t-intervals.

\textbf{Metric and rule.} The metric is ship AP50-95 (local linear-interpolation AP), the only class both detectors emit. One rule decides every registered verdict, on development and held-out data alike: an arm passes (development) or replicates (held-out) if no cell is worse than its baseline by 0.0014 or more with the interval below zero, and at least one cell is better by 0.0060 or more with the interval above zero. The 0.0014 floor is the measured two-sigma noise of a paired delta; 0.0060 is the floor widened by the measured autocorrelation inflation. On held-out cells the development grid did not contain, the same rule is a first test, not a replication.

\textbf{Registration.} Each arm's prediction, cells, statistic and rule were written and committed before any of its numbers existed. No constant, threshold or calibration of any system was fitted on held-out labels, but two gate constants were chosen with the held-out run's label-free statistics (Section~\ref{sec:4.4}), and no untouched test set existed before it. The held-out run is scored only through registered tests, and each scoring is logged in an exposure ledger. It has been scored thirteen times: the original look of the shipped system, a re-score of its corrupted cells after the corruption model was replaced, and eleven later registrations: one of the gate-free systems (\textsc{union} and \textsc{full\_tta}), seven adaptation tests (Section~\ref{sec:5.2}), two scorings of the gate ablation (Section~\ref{sec:5.1}) and one of shallow BN-mix (Section~\ref{sec:5.1}). The evidence record names the variants by registration codes (\mbox{IG-BN} = N4, \mbox{IG-BN-causal} = N4c2, \mbox{IG-BN-stale} = N4c, \mbox{IG-BN+glare} = N4g, \mbox{IG-BN+ens} = N4F, \mbox{IG-BN+ens+glare} = N4Fg, \mbox{IG-BN+AE} = N4ae).

\subsection{Backbone benchmark}\label{sec:3.5}
Ninety-three runs, 31 YOLO variants from six families with three seeds each, were trained on the corrected labels and stopped after 20 epochs without a new best mAP50-95. Table~\ref{tab:1} lists the YOLO26 top tier and the best variant of each other family. The YOLO26 m, l and x variants differ by at most 0.0040, below the larger seed standard deviation of every pair, so the benchmark resolves a tier, not an order; the best variants of the other five families sit 0.010--0.025 below yolo26m. The selection rule, fixed before the benchmark (the top tier, then a DFL head, then the simplest fork, then throughput), falls to throughput, where yolo26m runs at 57.0 frames per second against 30.7 for yolo26x. These are Ultralytics validation mAPs over ship and buoy on the full visible validation split, not the local ship AP of every other table, so no value here is comparable with them.

\section{Method}\label{sec:4}
\subsection{The ambiguity a single camera cannot resolve}\label{sec:4.1}
A degraded visible frame raises a question its own pixels cannot answer: is the scene dark, or is the camera failing? The visible health score is $q_{\mathrm{vis}}$ = min(1, 124.3/d$^{2}$), where d$^{2}$ is the Mahalanobis novelty of eleven frame statistics, fitted on clean day frames of the development runs, and 124.3 is its maximum over those frames; $q_{\mathrm{vis}}$ < 1 means d$^{2}$ > 124.3. The statistics are gradient Gini, mean gradient magnitude, the ratio of Laplacian variance to intensity variance, spectral slope, texture cover, the median ratio of local to global contrast, edge density, intensity standard deviation, the 5th-to-95th-percentile range, the log of the 95th-to-5th-percentile ratio and the fraction of dark pixels; the six heavy-tailed ones are log-compressed. It is a good detector of an unusual visible frame: it flags fogged, underexposed and noisy day frames. It is also, necessarily, a detector of night. On the development paired set it flags all 1,032 clean night frames as unhealthy and none of the 1,200 clean day frames. Night frames are in the visible detector's training distribution, and adapting them hurts (Section~\ref{sec:5.1}). The thermal image's 5th-percentile intensity separates the two cases on development: clean day frames lie between 2 and 34 and clean night frames between 49 and 113 on its 8-bit scale. Because each thermal frame is stretched to its own minimum and maximum, this is a statistic of the stretched image, not of scene temperature; we have not established how much of the separation comes from the stretch.

\subsection{The gate}\label{sec:4.2}
In plain terms, the gate adapts a frame when the visible image looks wrong and the thermal camera reports daytime and is itself working. Per frame and without labels, it activates when three conditions hold:
\begin{itemize}
\item the visible frame is flagged as unhealthy: $q_{\mathrm{vis}}$ < 1;
\item the thermal frame reads daylight: its 5th-percentile intensity $p_{05}^{\mathrm{IR}}$ $\leq$ 41.5, the midpoint of the empty margin between clean day and clean night on development;
\item the thermal frame is itself healthy: the Mahalanobis novelty of its own eleven frame statistics is within 222.7, its maximum over clean development frames.
\end{itemize}

The third term exists because a degraded thermal stream can misread the scene: after the per-frame stretch, thermal fog and noise move a frame's 5th percentile across the day--night threshold, and without the health term the gate leaks onto up to 2.2 percent of night frames under thermal fog. With it, the gate activates on no night frame under any thermal condition on development. The threshold 41.5 was fitted on the same development frames on which this separation is shown.

\subsection{The adaptation}\label{sec:4.3}
Frames are taken in non-overlapping blocks of eight consecutive frames. Where the gate activates, every BatchNorm layer of the visible detector normalizes with the BN-mix statistics of \citet{schneider2020improving}:
\begin{equation*}\mu = \frac{N\mu_{\mathrm{src}} + n\mu_b}{N+n},\qquad \sigma^2 = \frac{N\sigma^2_{\mathrm{src}} + n\sigma^2_b}{N+n},\end{equation*}
with N = 16, n = 8, and $\mu_b$, $\sigma^2_b$ the block's statistics over its frames and spatial positions, computed layer by layer as the block passes through the network. Frames the gate does not pass keep the detector's plain output. No gradient is computed, no weight changes, no label is read, and the thermal detector is never adapted; the two streams are then fused by \textsc{union}.

\subsection{Variants}\label{sec:4.4}
Table~\ref{tab:22} lists the baselines and every variant. \mbox{IG-BN} normalizes a block with its own statistics, which include up to seven later frames (0.7 s at 10 Hz); \mbox{IG-BN-causal} avoids this and is the version for a live stream. A first causal form, \mbox{IG-BN-stale}, reused the statistics of the previous block's adapted pass and failed by construction (Section~\ref{sec:5.1}). \mbox{IG-BN}'s gate almost never activates under glare, because a glared frame is bright and textured and does not look novel to $q_{\mathrm{vis}}$; the glare term covers that case. Shallow BN-mix drops the gate altogether. On every block it adapts only the first 31 of the detector's 130 BatchNorm layers, with the BN-mix weight n/(N + n) scaled by max(0, 1 $-$ D₀/D), where D is the block's divergence from the training statistics at that layer (mean symmetric KL over channels) and D₀ its median over 240 clean training blocks. A block that looks like training data is left unchanged, by day or night. The layer count and the median were chosen on one development draw before registration.

\textbf{Where the constants come from.} N = 16 and the gate's terms were chosen on a preliminary screening draw before any development verdict; N = 64 halved both the gains and the losses. The visible health bound, the thermal day threshold and the thermal health bound are the frozen constants of the shipped system, fitted on clean development frames. Two choices used the held-out run's label-free frame statistics before any of its scores existed. The thermal health term was switched from the shipped system's tighter bound, the 99th percentile of the same novelty over clean development frames, to its maximum (222.7) after the 99th-percentile bound was seen to pass only 9.5 percent of clean held-out thermal frames (the maximum passes 86.7 percent). The glare thresholds were checked to activate on 0.10 percent of clean held-out frames, after brightness percentiles that separate development glare perfectly were seen to activate on 55 percent of them. No constant was fitted on held-out labels.

\section{Results}\label{sec:5}
\subsection{Development}\label{sec:5.1}
\textbf{Ungated adaptation hurts.} In a preliminary screen on one corruption draw (two systems, not registered), BN-mix with N = 16 on every frame gained +0.0635 and +0.0767 ship AP on low-light day and +0.0088 and +0.0083 on fog by day, but lost 0.0080 and 0.0068 on clean day frames and up to 0.0311 at night. The gate is designed to keep the corrupted-frame gains and avoid the clean- and night-frame losses. A pre-registered ablation, below, confirms the losses and asks which part of the gate avoids them.

\textbf{IG-BN passes development} (Table~\ref{tab:2}). No cell of the 60 is worse than \textsc{union}; the worst $\Delta$ is $-$0.00001. Five are better beyond 0.0060 with intervals above zero: low light by day +0.0706 [+0.0593, +0.0818], low light with thermal fog at severity 1 +0.0357, fog at severity 1 +0.0094, fog at severity 2 +0.0091 and low light with thermal fog at severity 2 +0.0069. The gate activates on 16 cells, all by day: on 100 percent of low-light day frames and 99.6 percent of fogged day frames with clean thermal, and on no night frame under any thermal condition, so \mbox{IG-BN} equals \textsc{union} on every night cell. As thermal fog thickens the gate activates less, because the thermal stream no longer confirms daylight: on low-light day frames it activates on 42.5, 14.9 and 4.5 percent at thermal fog severities 1--3, and on none under thermal noise. Where fog degrades both bands, as real fog does, the gate therefore adapts few frames.

\textbf{The variants.} \mbox{IG-BN+glare} gains +0.0240 under glare by day and +0.0130 with the thermal stream in light fog; its worst cell is $-$0.0008. \mbox{IG-BN-stale} collapses from the first block that uses stale statistics, because they were measured under that block's own stale normalization rather than \mbox{IG-BN}'s: mean maximum confidence falls to 0.21 against \mbox{IG-BN}'s 0.75, and it was not taken further. \mbox{IG-BN-causal} passes; against \mbox{IG-BN} the price of causality is $-$0.0038 [$-$0.0045, $-$0.0031] on low-light day and within $\pm$0.0003 on fog. \mbox{IG-BN+AE} gains +0.0165 [+0.0053, +0.0278] over \mbox{IG-BN} on low light by day; darkness splits the conditions exactly, since every gated low-light frame is dark and no gated fog frame is, so on fog \mbox{IG-BN+AE} is \mbox{IG-BN}. Inside the ensemble, \mbox{IG-BN+ens}'s gain survives almost undiminished (+0.0696 on low-light day, on its own draws), and so does the glare gain (\mbox{IG-BN+ens+glare}, +0.0179 on glare by day). \mbox{IG-BN+ens+glare}'s rule had no gain requirement: no cell worse than \textsc{full\_tta}, and none below \mbox{IG-BN+ens} by 0.0014 where the glare term adds frames. The held-out build runs in half precision with fused batch statistics; a development check put its effect at no more than 0.0003.

\textbf{Which part of the gate does the work.} A pre-registered ablation scored the same adaptation under nine other gates. On development every prediction held: without a day--night term adaptation loses at night (to $-$0.0233), as does the feature-distribution gap of \citet{yoo2024what}, which activates on 90--100 percent of night frames. The day--night term need not come from the thermal camera: the visible term with solar elevation is worse than \mbox{IG-BN} on no cell and better on 13, every degraded day cell with a corrupted thermal stream (+0.0709 [+0.0592, +0.0825] in low light under thermal noise). On the held-out daylight run, adapting every frame beats \mbox{IG-BN} on eight of nine cells (+0.0202 to +0.0216 on clean-visible cells), against the registered prediction. One untested explanation is that development's clean frames come from the training runs, while the held-out run is a separate recording whose clean frames are themselves slightly shifted (Section~\ref{sec:7}). The sun is up on every held-out frame, so the held-out run cannot test the clock: there the clock gate is the ungated arm.

\textbf{Adapting without any gate.} Shallow BN-mix (Section~\ref{sec:4.4}) needs neither a thermal camera nor a clock. It was registered on development draws 942--944 after a screen on draw 941. No cell is worse than \textsc{union} and 24 are better; against \mbox{IG-BN} it is better on 22 cells and worse on 2. It wins where \mbox{IG-BN}'s gate stays off: in light visible fog with a degraded thermal stream (+0.0174 to +0.0212, against at most +0.0006 for \mbox{IG-BN}) and in low light by day under thermal fog or noise (+0.0558 to +0.0590, against at most +0.0069), because it does not depend on the thermal stream. It loses where \mbox{IG-BN} adapts every frame: low light by day ($-$0.0126 against \mbox{IG-BN}) and fog by day ($-$0.0033). Clean day frames move by at most 0.0002. Night is its weak side: clean and low-light night cells lie between $-$0.0046 and $-$0.0021, every interval crossing zero, within the registered $\pm$0.005 band. On the held-out run (a thirteenth registered scoring), it replicates (3 cells better, none worse): noise +0.1789, fog +0.0377 and low light +0.0088 over \textsc{union}. It is below \mbox{IG-BN} in low light ($-$0.0099) and, as registered, does not take the ungated arm's gain on clean held-out frames ($-$0.0003 against \textsc{union}; below ungated BN-mix on all nine cells).

Fog, low light and glare repeat development conditions and are replications; sensor noise, rain and blur are first tests.

\textbf{IG-BN.} No cell is worse than \textsc{union}, and three are better beyond 0.0060 with intervals above zero. Under visible sensor noise, re-estimating the normalization statistics takes the fused output from 0.0169 to 0.1992; the ten-pass \textsc{full\_tta} reaches only 0.0206 there. This is the established benefit of BN re-estimation under noise \cite{schneider2020improving}, and a first test, since development has no visible noise. Fog gains +0.0370 and low light +0.0186, as on development. On the four cells with a clean visible stream (thermal clean, blurred, noisy or fogged) the gate activates on no frame, so \mbox{IG-BN} is \textsc{union} there. Because every held-out frame is daylight and every adaptation cell has a clean thermal stream, these cells exercise the gate's visible term; its day--night term is tested only on development night (Section~\ref{sec:5.3}).

\textbf{IG-BN-causal.} The causal version keeps \mbox{IG-BN}'s held-out gains, with no cell worse: against \mbox{IG-BN} it costs at most 0.0007 (fog) on the held-out run and 0.0038 on development low light. With the glare term (\mbox{IG-BN-causal+glare}) it replicates on glare, 0.0003 below \mbox{IG-BN+glare}.

\textbf{IG-BN+glare.} None of the nine registered cells corrupts the visible stream with glare, so its registration added a tenth. There \mbox{IG-BN+glare} gains +0.0309 [+0.0290, +0.0327] over \textsc{union} (0.1417 to 0.1726), where \mbox{IG-BN} alone gains nothing, as on development; in the three other cells where the glare term adds two or three gated frames per draw, \mbox{IG-BN+glare} equals \mbox{IG-BN} to the fourth decimal.

\textbf{IG-BN+ens.} Inside the ensemble, no cell is worse than \textsc{full\_tta}. The gain is larger than \mbox{IG-BN}'s alone under noise (+0.2174 against +0.1823; 0.0206 to 0.2380) and fog (+0.0445 against +0.0370; 0.0586 to 0.1031), and the same under low light (+0.0190 against +0.0186) and rain (+0.0033 against +0.0036). Under glare, \mbox{IG-BN}'s gate activates on 1.9 percent of frames and \mbox{IG-BN+ens} equals \textsc{full\_tta}, so glare was registered separately with the glare term (\mbox{IG-BN+ens+glare}, after a development pass). It replicates: +0.0311 [+0.0286, +0.0332] over \textsc{full\_tta} (0.1656 to 0.1967), +0.0240 above one-pass \mbox{IG-BN+glare}, with no other cell worse than \mbox{IG-BN+ens}. On five of the six held-out cells with a corrupted visible stream, \mbox{IG-BN+ens} (\mbox{IG-BN+ens+glare} on glare) is the highest-scoring system we measured; under blur it ties \textsc{full\_tta}.

\textbf{IG-BN+AE, with a cost development could not show.} Low light gains +0.0259 [+0.0231, +0.0285] over \textsc{union}, +0.0073 [+0.0046, +0.0099] over \mbox{IG-BN}, as on development. But the held-out rain darkens every gated rain frame below auto-exposure's threshold, so auto-exposure replaces adaptation there and \mbox{IG-BN+AE} on rain is 0.0036 below \mbox{IG-BN}. Development has no rain. We do not recommend \mbox{IG-BN+AE} for that reason.

\subsection{Where the gate does not activate}\label{sec:5.3}
The gate's job is as much where it stays off as where it activates. It activates on no frame of the clean held-out cell, on a rounded 0.0 percent of the other clean-visible held-out cells, and on no development night frame under any thermal condition, so on those frames every variant equals its baseline. That matters because the baseline is already strong there. At night, \textsc{union} keeps the visible stream that the shipped veto discards. On a night test registered on pohang01's test split, 1,109 frame pairs that no fusion system had scored, \textsc{union} beats \textsc{shipped} by +0.0273 [+0.0154, +0.0400] and holds the no-loss property at $-$0.0010 [$-$0.0049, +0.0031], while \textsc{shipped}, which vetoes the visible stream on 90.3 percent of those frames, fails it by 0.0283. The detectors trained on the same run's training split, so this tests the fusion rule, not the detectors, and night AP levels swing from 0.04 to 0.35 between the run's 52-second episodes; directions, not levels, transfer. On these 1,109 pairs \mbox{IG-BN}'s gate, measured without labels, activates on none with a clean or noisy thermal stream and on one pair in one of nine thermal-fog draws, 1 of 17,744 pair-draws in all. \mbox{IG-BN} thus equals \textsc{union} on this night test. The registered prediction was that the gate would activate on no pair; it fails by that one pair. The thermal terms do not hold the line alone: under thermal fog the thermal stream reads day on 37--42 percent of these night pairs, and the health term rejects all but the one. A solar gate activates on none (the sun is 6--10$^{\circ}$ below the horizon), the feature-gap gate of Section~\ref{sec:5.1} on 99.3 percent (Yoo et al.'s thresholds) or 66.5 percent (calibrated).

\subsection{An observation, not a test: ranking the adapted streams}\label{sec:5.4}
\mbox{IG-BN} inherits a weakness of \textsc{union}. Where the visible stream is clean, the fused output falls below the visible stream alone, by 0.0085 to 0.0132 on the held-out run, because the thermal stream's boxes are interleaved with the visible stream's. A fixed ordering that ranks every visible box above every thermal box (\textsc{lex}) cannot fall below the visible stream: the scorer matches boxes greedily in score order, so a tail of boxes appended below every existing box cannot lower AP (Section~\ref{sec:6.3}). The same ordering of \mbox{IG-BN}'s adapted streams scores above \mbox{IG-BN} in all nine held-out cells, by +0.0096 to +0.0134 where the visible stream is clean and +0.0008 to +0.0067 where it is corrupted, and it holds the no-loss property in every cell. No verdict was registered for it, and on development \textsc{lex} averaged 0.0037 below \textsc{union} over the 60 cells. The two data sets disagree, so we report it as a candidate for the next registration and recommend \mbox{IG-BN} with \textsc{union}, as registered. The visible detector with \mbox{IG-BN} and no thermal boxes at all was not scored as a system.

\section{What did not work on the same system}\label{sec:6}
The adaptation was the last of a sequence of registered attempts to use the second sensor. The earlier ones are what made its design plain, and we summarize them here.

\subsection{Predicted uncertainty is informative but does not improve the fusion}\label{sec:6.1}
Each detector carries a Gaussian variance head \cite{choi2019gaussian} trained with a beta-weighted negative log-likelihood \cite{seitzer2022on}, and the system was designed so that predicted $\sigma$ would weight the fusion. We pre-registered the comparison that answers whether it should: real $\sigma$ against the same $\sigma$ shuffled onto the wrong boxes, at least three of four conditions above 0.0060 with a block-bootstrap interval excluding zero. Used as a weight on box coordinates, $\sigma$ passes on none of four conditions, and the system's fusion weight was measured to take one value on every frame. Used to re-rank scores, real $\sigma$ beats shuffled $\sigma$ on three of four conditions, so it carries information about which boxes are right. But that information is within each detector: by day the gain is the visible detector re-ranking its own boxes, and adding the thermal stream moves it by $-$0.0040 to +0.0035 with no consistent sign. Against the system with no $\sigma$ at all, the re-ranked system scores lower on six of eight cells. A shuffled control establishes that a signal exists, not that using it helps. Learned jointly with confidence in a re-ranker of the visible boxes, $\sigma$ adds +0.0050 [+0.0038, +0.0064] on one checkpoint, and its pre-registered replication on the five retrained detectors failed: positive on all five, beyond the floor on two. Two further lessons came from this test. The recorded runs had scored a ship-and-buoy macro instead of the registered ship AP, and the macro showed no effect of score re-ranking where ship AP showed a pass; checking that the scored quantity is the registered one belongs in the registration. Under physically modeled corruptions, re-ranking passes on only one or two of four conditions.

\subsection{A sensor veto is a claim about the detector}\label{sec:6.2}
The system that shipped dropped the visible stream when the thermal camera voted night and the visible frame read dark or veiled. Its night arm was written while the visible detector scored 0.0000 at night. That zero turned out to be a label artifact: a filter had deleted every box in dark night frames from the training labels, and a registered restore of the boxes took night visible mAP50-95 from 0.0000 to 0.2520. Retrained on the corrected labels, the visible detector sees at night, and the unchanged rule throws it away: on clean night the fused output equals the thermal stream alone and falls 0.1847 [0.1655, 0.2039] below the visible stream. Nothing in the image changed; what changed is the claim the rule makes about the detector. The rule gated on darkness, while what decides whether the visible stream should be dropped is its health, and with the retrained detector those variables no longer coincide. The same confusion appears on the thermal side: under a fogged or noisy thermal stream, the veto's fallback reads a dark low-light day as a fogged night and vetoes a working visible stream on up to 96 percent of day frames. The adaptation's gate keeps the two questions apart: it asks the thermal camera whether it is day, and each stream whether it is healthy.

\subsection{No learned gate beat removing the veto}\label{sec:6.3}
Seven learned or hand-written replacements for the veto were registered and scored on fresh corruption draws, from per-stream calibration and Bayesian pair fusion to gradient-boosted trust over 32 backbone features. None beat switching the veto off: \textsc{union} is better than \textsc{shipped} on 30 of 60 development cells and worse on none, and every gate was worse than \textsc{shipped} somewhere by day. Two mechanisms explain most of it. A model of box correctness fitted to a noisy matching target re-orders a detector's own boxes worse than its confidence does. And a frame-level gate pools frames whose scores live on different scales: switching to the visible stream alone on a random three quarters of frames, a choice that carries no information, scores 0.0085 below the interpolation between the two pure policies. What worked used the scorer's structure. Boxes appended below every existing box cannot lower AP, so demoting a stream is never worse than deleting it, and a fixed tier order holds the floor of the better stream by construction (\textsc{lex}, Section~\ref{sec:5.4}). The largest gain needed no fusion idea at all: ensembling frozen checkpoints helps every arm it is put under, and \textsc{full\_tta} beats \textsc{shipped} on 57 of 60 development cells and on all nine held-out cells. The adaptation is the one change in this sequence that acts inside a detector, and it adds to the ensemble rather than competing with it.

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:7}
\textbf{What the thermal camera contributes, and what is not yet shown.} As a second detector scored against the visible labels, the thermal stream adds little by day on this data: on the held-out run it scores 0.0156 against the visible stream's 0.2767, and fusing it lowers the output wherever the visible stream is clean (Section~\ref{sec:5.4}). That comparison is confounded: the held-out run has visible labels only, so a true thermal-only detection counts as a false positive, and against its own labels on development the thermal detector scores 0.141 ship AP by day, against the visible detector's 0.378 on the same frames; the 0.05 percent partner rate at IoU 0.85 (Section~\ref{sec:3.2}) may reflect cross-camera box correspondence as much as weak sensing. As a gate, the thermal camera separated a dark scene from a degraded camera on development, where an underexposed visible frame and a night frame look alike to every statistic of the visible frame we tried. The pre-registered ablation (Section~\ref{sec:5.1}) shows that the separation is needed and that the thermal camera is not needed to make it. A solar clock in place of the thermal terms is never worse than \mbox{IG-BN} and is better on 13 development cells, those where a corrupted thermal stream no longer confirms daylight. The thermal reading would earn its place only where a clock is wrong about the light the camera sees: dusk, dawn, heavy overcast, bridges and covered berths. None occur in this data. The held-out run also questions the visible term: there, adapting every daylight frame beat \mbox{IG-BN} and the clock gate by about 0.02 on clean frames, so development's clean-frame losses, on frames from the training runs, may overstate the cost of adapting clean-looking frames.

\textbf{What we recommend.} For a two-stream detector built from frozen detectors: fuse by \textsc{union}, without a night veto. Do not adapt the visible detector at night. By day, adapt with BN-mix, in its causal form for a live stream, and where ten detector passes per stream are affordable, inside an ensemble of frozen checkpoints with flipped views. Decide day and night with a solar clock where position and time are known; on this data it served better than the thermal reading, and a thermal reading of daylight needs its own health check, since thermal fog makes it read day on up to 42 percent of night frames (Section~\ref{sec:5.3}). On whether to adapt every daylight frame or only flagged ones, development and the held-out run disagree (Section~\ref{sec:5.1}); \mbox{IG-BN}, used in every held-out replication in Table~\ref{tab:3}, is the conservative choice. Where no day--night signal is available, shallow BN-mix adapts without one and was worse than \textsc{union} on no development or held-out cell, at a small cost at night and less gain in low light (Section~\ref{sec:5.1}). Ranking visible boxes above thermal ones is a candidate, not a recommendation (Section~\ref{sec:5.4}).

\textbf{A note on the protocol.} A measured paired noise floor, block-bootstrap intervals and magnitude floors moved 20 of 74 earlier findings of this project to indeterminate when applied retroactively, and a registration exposed a wrong metric in its own recorded runs (Section~\ref{sec:6.1}). The adaptation's gains survive these corrections by an order of magnitude: the smallest headline gain, +0.0186, is nearly eight times the 0.0024 maximum of the ship-AP noise floor.

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:8}
Test-time adaptation of a visible detector is easy to apply and hard to aim: on our development set it helped on degraded frames and hurt on clean and night frames, and a visible camera cannot tell a dark scene from a dark sensor. Gating BatchNorm re-estimation on a co-mounted thermal camera's reading of daylight and on both streams' health kept the gains with no development or held-out cell worse. With every test pre-registered, it passed development and replicated in direction on one held-out daylight run under fog (+0.037 ship AP), low light (+0.019) and glare (+0.031), and gained +0.18 under sensor noise in a first test; its causal form cost at most 0.0038 on development and 0.0007 on the held-out run, and inside a ten-pass ensemble its gains added under noise and fog and held elsewhere. A pre-registered ablation then showed that the gate needs its day--night term but not the thermal camera: a solar clock served at least as well. The same system's earlier attempts to use the second sensor, as an uncertainty-weighted voter and as a sensor veto, did not survive registration.

\textbf{Data and code availability.} The Pohang Canal images and PoLaRIS labels are public \cite{chung2023pohang,choi2025polaris}. The code, every pre-registration as a dated commit, the exposure ledger and the result record behind each table and figure are in the public repository github.com/Laksh-saroha/maritime-tta.
